title: An optimized permeabilization step for flow cytometry analysis of nuclear proteins in myeloid differentiation of blood cells into neutrophils
author: Viryasova, Golenkina, et al.

steps.title: Isolate neutrophils from blood
steps.instruction: Isolate neutrophils from healthy donor blood using 3 % dextran followed by Ficoll‑Paque density gradient centrifugation; confirm purity by CD66b flow cytometry. Because neutrophils may be lost during preparation, collect 2–3 × the intended cell number.

steps.title: Culture and differentiate HL‑60 cells
steps.instruction: Grow HL‑60 cells in RPMI‑1640 medium supplemented with HEPES, sodium bicarbonate, 10 % FBS and 2 mM L‑glutamine until the culture reaches 1 × 10⁶ cells · mL⁻¹. Induce differentiation by adding 2 mM all‑trans retinoic acid (ATRA) and incubate according to standard protocols. Verify differentiation by CD66b flow cytometry. Prepare 2 × 10⁶ cells per experimental sample.

steps.title: Fix cells with paraformaldehyde
steps.instruction: Fix both neutrophils and HL‑60 cells with 2 % (or 2–4 %) para‑formaldehyde (PFA) solution at room temperature for the standard fixation time used in your laboratory.

steps.title: Permeabilize with ice‑cold ethanol
steps.instruction: Permeabilize the fixed cells by adding ice‑cold 70 % ethanol and incubating on ice for 30 min. Do not store neutrophils after this step at +4 °C or –20 °C; HL‑60 cells may be stored if needed.

steps.title: Add protease/phosphatase inhibitors (optional)
steps.instruction: Prepare all buffer solutions (including the ethanol permeabilization buffer) with the following inhibitors added before and after permeabilization: 2 mM DFP, 50 µM zVAD, protease inhibitor cocktail (1 : 50 dilution), phosphatase inhibitor cocktail III (1 : 100 dilution).

steps.title: Block non‑specific binding
steps.instruction: Block cells in PBS containing 1 % BSA. For HL‑60 cells incubate 30 min at room temperature. For neutrophils add 10 % non‑immune goat serum to the 1 % BSA/PBS solution and incubate 30 min at room temperature.

steps.title: Primary antibody staining
steps.instruction: Resuspend the cell pellet in 100 µL PBS + 1 % BSA (staining buffer). Wait 10 min, then add the primary antibody at the required concentration. Incubate 30–40 min at room temperature. Add 2.5 mL staining buffer, then centrifuge at 300 g, 4 °C for 6 min.

steps.title: Secondary antibody staining
steps.instruction: Resuspend the pellet in 200 µL staining buffer containing the appropriate secondary antibody. Incubate 30 min in the dark at room temperature. Centrifuge at 300 g, 4 °C for 6 min, wash with 1 mL PBS, centrifuge again at 300 g, 4 °C for 6 min, and finally resuspend the cells in 350 µL PBS.

steps.title: Acquire flow cytometry data
steps.instruction: Analyze the stained cells on a flow cytometer, collecting data for the nuclear protein of interest (e.g., GFI1) and appropriate isotype controls.

description: Flow cytometry (FACS) is a well-known method widely used for many tasks, e.g. intracellular and cell surface molecular detection, with such advantages as multiparametric analysis, semi-quantitative data analysis, statistical reliability and relatively easy sample preparation [3]. To evaluate changes in protein expression during differentiation of promyelocytes into leukocytes we created a model system "HL-60 cells - differentiated with trans-retinoic acid (ATRA) HL-60 cell - primary neutrophils" [2]. The HL-60 cells are identified as acute promyelocytic leukemia cells [4]. Presently they were described as promyelocytes or myeloblasts and are well known as model system for studying myeloid cell differentiation [5]. Working with primary human neutrophils is complicated because of many specific properties, high sensitivity to permeabilization agents and impossibility of sample storage. Thus, for this investigation we had to elaborate а universal flow cytometry protocol, which would allow comparison of the nuclear protein expression data obtained in neutrophils and in HL-60 cells. Various activators and transcriptional complexes are responsible for gene expression, which are also changing in the process of differentiation [6]. Changes in the levels of transcription activators may lead to various diseases such as leukemia [7]. To validate suggested protocol improvements, we measured the changes in GFI1 protein expression, which is known to be primarily important in myeloid and lymphoid differentiation. GFI1-deficient mice show a block in myeloid differentiation, an accumulation of myelomonocytic cells, and an expansion of GMPs, which are myeloid progenitors known to cause acute promyelocytic leukemia [8]. GFI1 promotes differentiation in myeloid cells and is crucial for late-stage neutrophil production [9].
